newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Democrats urged to work with China on handover.
newsitem.headline: HK Democrats urged to work with China on handover.

text.p: Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping tycoon strongly tipped to become the territory's first chief executive, on Friday urged the territory's Democratic Party not to seek confrontation with China.
"The Democratic Party shouldn't be confrontational towards China regarding its dealing in Hong Kong and Chinese affairs," Tung told reporters after meeting party leaders at their headquarters.
Tung's call came after the Democratic Party said it would seek talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen during his visit to Hong Kong on November 15.

Tung, regarded as Beijing's favourite to take over from Governor Chris Patten when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1 next year, said the democrats should join the controversial provisional legislature for the good of Hong Kong.
"They should join the provisional legislature," he said. "But even if they are not joining, they should give positive support to the provisional body."

The Democratic Party, a vocal critic of Chinese policies, has been branded subversive by Beijing and sidelined from the power structures that China is crafting to run the territory after the handover at midnight on June 30.
The party, which with 19 seats in the 60-seat Legislative Council is the largest political faction in the chamber, has said it will not join the interim legislature that will be installed on July 1.

China, upset by electoral reforms introduced by Patten, has vowed to scrap the elected Legislative Council and replace it with the provisional body until fresh elections in 1998. The pro-democracy camp in Hong Kong has condemned the plan as seeking to snuff out democracy in the territory.
Tung said the community as a whole should be united in working towards Hong Kong's smooth transition from a British colony to a Special Administrative Region of China.
Democratic Party vice-chairman Szeto Wah reiterated his party's position on the interim body.
"We will not join the provisional legislature. It's a matter of principle," Szeto told a news conference after the meeting.
He said his party would cooperate on other transitional matters but did not elaborate.
"We have sent a letter to Mr Qian asking him for a meeting when he is in Hong Kong," Szeto said. "We would like to have a face-to-face discussion with him on matters concerning the handover."
Another democrat, Yeung Sum, was critical of Tung, saying he would be puppet of China if he became the post-1997 chief.
"I think he will follow quite closely (the) Chinese policy regarding civil liberties, human rights, democracy and Chinese dissidents," he said.
The other front-runners in the race for chief executive are former Hong Kong Chief Justice Ti Liang Yang, former Appeal Court judge Simon Li and businessman Peter Woo.
The chief executive will be chosen by a 400-member China-appointed selection committee in Hong Kong on December 11.
